paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: Lin Min-Ju's first job began with somebody else's work. The company that hired her was a small online clothing retailer in Taipei, and its website had grown much faster than the team that looked after it. The developer who had built the site — and who understood every page of it — was leaving, so on Min-Ju's first morning her manager placed a thick folder on her desk. "Yi-Chen wrote all of this before she left," he said. "Read it first. We'll talk afterwards."

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: The note at the top of the first page, however, was the shortest thing in the folder. It was a single underlined sentence: “You must read all of this before you change anything.” Min-Ju smiled at it the way new employees smile at warnings, and then she turned the page.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: By the end of the morning she understood the shape of the whole site: the front-end pages that customers clicked, and the back-end services that stored their orders and turned them into deliveries. There was a framework Yi-Chen had chosen years earlier, a set of approved wireframe drawings from the design team, and one promise that applied to every page — it had to stay responsive on any screen, including the older phones most customers actually used. Two pages, Min-Ju discovered, had been rewritten simply because a customer using a screen reader could not buy anything on them. After that, accessibility appeared in the notes again and again.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: Three weeks later, the whole team gathered to watch the new site go live. The deploy itself took less than a minute, but Min-Ju kept the tab open all afternoon, typing the domain name from memory and watching the familiar front page appear. Only then did she understand that she had not been given a folder of notes. She had been given a way of working — something a stranger could read on her first day and follow. Four years of somebody else's rules had kept the site alive long enough for those rules to become the most valuable thing in the folder.

paragraphs.text: These modals all talk about obligation, but they differ in how strong the obligation is and where it comes from.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: The classic error: mustn't does NOT mean ‘don't have to’.✗ You mustn't update the content every day. (= it is forbidden)→ ✓ You don't have to update the content every day. (= it is not necessary)Also, there is no to after a modal: ✗ I must to go. → ✓ I must go.
